title: Multi-Agent Decomposition: Splitting by Domain vs by Platform Limit

steps.prompt: An enterprise is building Agentforce support for Billing Disputes, Technical Support, and Sales Quoting. The three domains need 20 topics in total, averaging 12 actions each, and each request belongs to one domain. How should the architect structure the agents?

options.label: Three domain agents under an orchestrator limited to classifying intent and routing
options.rationale: Orchestration should stay narrow: the orchestrator picks the specialist, and the task reasoning happens in the agent that holds that domain's context and actions. Splitting by domain also keeps each agent under the 15-topic limit that 20 topics would exceed in a single agent.

options.label: Three domain agents under an orchestrator that plans each full resolution before delegating
options.rationale: Planning in the orchestrator duplicates reasoning that belongs in the specialist with the domain context, so every request is reasoned about twice and pays for it in tokens.

options.label: One agent with the 20 topics merged into 15 broader, cross-domain topics
options.rationale: An agent holds at most 15 topics of up to 15 actions each, so 15 topics cannot carry about 240 actions; broader topics would also blend domains and blur classification.

options.label: Enough agents that none holds more than 15 actions, all under one orchestrator
options.rationale: The 15-action limit applies per topic, not per agent, so splitting by action count creates about 16 agents where three fit, and each agent draws its own governor limits.
